input.title: Hybrid Compression for Memory-Efficient Matrix-Vector Multiplication
input.summary: Iterative machine-learning algorithms repeatedly access large real-valued matrices through matrix-vector products, and their performance is limited by memory bandwidth rather than arithmetic throughput. Lossless compression schemes that support computation directly over the compressed data reduce both the data moved and the memory footprint of these workloads. The mm-RePair framework [11] follows this approach by applying the RePair grammar compressor to the Compressed Sparse Row/Value (CSRV) representation of a matrix and performing matrix-vector multiplications directly on the compressed data. Its effectiveness, however, degrades on matrices that are dense or contain many distinct values. In this paper we present a hybrid strategy for the mm-RePair framework that combines grammar and entropy compression. The CSRV sequence is partitioned into a grammar-compressible component, formed by the entries that mm-RePair can compress effectively, and an entropy-compressible component holding the remaining entries, which is encoded with the ans-fold coder [24]. Compression improves further by sorting and delta encoding the entries of each row in the CSRV representation, and by remapping the alphabet to a contiguous range. Experiments on real-valued machine-learning matrices, including word embeddings and transformer hidden states, show that our hybrid strategy is more compact than the original \mmRepair on every input and reduces the peak memory of multiplication, with the largest gains on dense matrices with many distinct values, at competitive multiplication times. It also outperforms the column-reordering variant of \mmRepair on most of the matrices, and combining the two is even more compact on the sparse ones, at the cost of a much longer compression time. Finally, our strategy scales with the number of threads as well as the original \mmRepair does.

input.title: From Retouched Images to Paired Videos: A Synthetic Benchmark for Face Video Retouching
input.summary: Paired unretouched/retouched face videos are costly to produce because professional editing must remain consistent over time, while releasing identifiable face footage raises privacy, consent, and governance concerns. We present DeepVFR, an initial controlled synthetic benchmark-not a new retouching architecture-for paired face video retouching. Starting from paired synthetic DeepFRR images, Wan2.2 generates mild-motion source clips, and backend-specific face transfer constructs synchronized proxy retouching targets, followed by automatic validity screening and manual visual inspection. DeepVFR contains 1,024 pairs of 150-frame clips at 30 fps, evaluated under an identity-disjoint protocol with explicit frame correspondence; release metadata will record the construction route. Within-benchmark baselines, external checkpoints applied to DeepVFR, qualitative analysis, and a 17-participant ranking study establish reference behavior in the controlled domain. The constructed targets exhibit a substantial low-preference tail in the human study. Because both streams inherit synthetic content and the targets additionally inherit commercial-API or face-transfer artifacts, the benchmark neither replaces artist-retouched captured video nor establishes synthetic-to-real generalization. DeepVFR provides a starting point for paired supervision and controlled evaluation. Data, individual study rankings, and training logs will be made publicly available upon acceptance. Broader motion coverage and real-video validation remain future work.

input.title: Mechanistic Interpretability of Mambas Selective Gate in Financial Markets: A Leakage-Controlled Study
input.summary: Selectively gated state-space models (SSMs), notably Mamba, are increasingly used for financial time series, yet how they internally represent market regimes (bull, bear, sideways) remains opaque. This paper applies Mechanistic Interpretability (MI) to a six-layer Mamba trained on approximately twenty-one years of daily data for a point-in-time set of S&P 500 constituents plus macroeconomic and Fama-French factors, decomposing per-layer hidden states with Top-K Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs). Our central contribution is methodological and cautionary. A prior, uncontrolled configuration recovered market regimes from SAE features at F1 = 1.00. Under a controlled protocol that (i) removes the three input features that overlap the HMM label definition, (ii) disables the auxiliary regime-classification head, (iii) uses a point-in-time constituent universe, and (iv) evaluates against labels disjoint from the inputs, the same regime label is recovered at only F1 = 0.398, indistinguishable from a logistic baseline on raw inputs (0.435) and from an SAE trained on a randomly initialized, untrained Mamba (0.364). A 2x2 attribution grid shows the near-perfect result is an interaction of auxiliary supervision and label-defining inputs: neither factor alone exceeds F1 ~ 0.40. Effect sizes with block-bootstrap inference show the residual selective-gate (Delta t) regime effect is statistically detectable but economically negligible and uniform across layers rather than layer-specialized; the apparent polysemanticity gradient disappears under continuous, theory-grounded measures. We contribute a reproducible leakage-control protocol for interpretability evaluation of financial SSMs, a quantified demonstration that previously reported regime structure is a label-contamination artifact, and a modest economically grounded feature subset that genuinely survives the controls.
